Biochemistry I — Chapter 2 Water

Drill version — tap a blank or a blurred figure to check the answer

2-0Overview

Water makes up ~70% of most organisms by weight. Its unusual properties — cohesion, high heat capacity, excellent solvent for polar/ionic substances — come from its ability to form hydrogen bonds.

2-1Physical Properties of Water

📄 Textbook page p.24 — text could not be extracted, shown as a page image

2-1A Water Is a Polar Molecule

Decision flow
  1. O is more electronegative than H → O carries δ⁻, the H atoms δ⁺
  2. Bent geometry (H–O–H ≈ 104.5°) → net dipole moment
  3. Each water can donate 2 and accept 2 H-bonds → up to 4 H-bonds (tetrahedral)

The O atom is sp³-like, with two nonbonding electron pairs; O–H bond length 0.958 Å; H–O–H angle 104.5°.

A hydrogen bond is a mainly electrostatic interaction between an H attached to an electronegative atom (the donor, e.g., O–H, N–H) and a lone pair of another electronegative atom (the acceptor). Energy ≈ 20 kJ·mol⁻¹ (vs. 460 kJ·mol⁻¹ for a covalent O–H bond); H···O distance ≈ 1.8 Å.

In ice, every water makes 4 H-bonds in an open hexagonal lattice → ice is less dense than liquid water and floats. Liquid water keeps most H-bonds but they rapidly break and reform (lifetime ~ picoseconds) — “flickering clusters”.

Noncovalent interactions (weak but numerous): ionic (electrostatic) interactions, hydrogen bonds, and van der Waals forces — dipole–dipole, dipole–induced dipole, and London dispersion forces (weakest, between any atoms).

Coulomb's law: U = kq₁q₂/Dr. The dielectric constant D is 1 in vacuum, 1.5–3 in hydrocarbons and 78.5 in water → water greatly weakens ionic attractions.

2-1B Hydrophilic Substances Dissolve in Water

Ions dissolve because water molecules orient their dipoles around them — solvation (hydration) — and the high dielectric constant shields the charges. Na⁺ is surrounded by the O (δ⁻) ends, Cl⁻ by the H (δ⁺) ends.

Polar molecules with H-bonding groups (hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, amino…) are hydrophilic and dissolve by forming H-bonds with water.

2-1C The Hydrophobic Effect Causes Nonpolar Substances to Aggregate in Water

Decision flow
  1. Nonpolar solute in water → water forms an ordered “cage” around it (to keep H-bonds)
  2. Ordering lowers water's entropy (−TΔS large and positive for dissolving)
  3. Nonpolar molecules aggregate → fewer ordered waters → entropy of water increases
  4. Hydrophobic effect = entropy-driven exclusion of nonpolar groups from water

Transferring a hydrocarbon from water to a nonpolar solvent has ΔH ≈ 0 or even positive, but −TΔS is large and negative → ΔG < 0 (Table 2-2). So the driving force is entropic, not an attraction between nonpolar molecules.

Amphiphilic (amphipathic) molecules have both polar and nonpolar parts, e.g., fatty acid anions (soaps: palmitate, oleate). In water they form micelles (tails inside) or bilayers (basis of biological membranes).

“Hydrophobic bonds” is a misnomer: nonpolar groups associate not because they attract each other strongly but because this maximizes the entropy of water.

2-1D Water Moves by Osmosis and Solutes Move by Diffusion

Osmosis: water moves across a semipermeable membrane from low to high solute concentration. The osmotic pressure needed to stop it is π = iMRT (i = ions per solute molecule, M = molarity).

Cells in a hypotonic solution swell (animal cells may burst; plant cells are protected by the cell wall); in a hypertonic solution they shrink.

Diffusion: net movement of solutes from high to low concentration by random motion. Dialysis uses a membrane that lets small solutes pass while retaining macromolecules — used to change the buffer of a protein sample.

2-2Chemical Properties of Water

2-2A Water Ionizes to Form H⁺ and OH⁻

H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻. The ion product Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ M² at 25°C. In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M. (H⁺ actually exists as hydronium H₃O⁺.)

H⁺ and OH⁻ move unusually fast in water by proton jumping — protons hop along chains of H-bonded water molecules (Grotthuss mechanism), not by the ion itself diffusing.

2-2B Acids and Bases Alter the pH

pH = −log[H⁺]. pH < 7 acidic, pH 7 neutral, pH > 7 basic. Blood ≈ 7.4, gastric juice ≈ 1.5.

Brønsted definitions: an acid is a proton donor, a base a proton acceptor. HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ — HA and A⁻ are a conjugate acid–base pair.

Dissociation constant K = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]; pK = −log K. The stronger the acid, the larger K and the smaller pK. Strong acids (HCl) dissociate completely; weak acids only partly.

Box 2-1 Ocean acidification: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; rising atmospheric CO₂ lowers ocean pH, and H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻ reduces the carbonate available for CaCO₃ shells.

2-2C Buffers Resist Changes in pH

Decision flow
  1. Weak acid HA + conjugate base A⁻ → use Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pK + log([A⁻]/[HA])
  2. [A⁻] = [HA] (midpoint of titration) → pH = pK
  3. Effective buffering range ≈ pK ± 1 pH unit
  4. Polyprotic acid → one buffering region (and one pK) per ionizable proton

Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK + log ([A⁻]/[HA]). When [A⁻] = [HA], pH = pK.

A titration curve is flattest at its midpoint (pH = pK): here added H⁺ or OH⁻ changes the pH least → a buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its pK.

Polyprotic acids (e.g., H₃PO₄) have several pK values: 2.15, 6.82, 12.38. The H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻ pair (pK 6.82) buffers inside cells.

Blood buffer (Box 2-2): CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, overall pK = 6.35. Lungs remove CO₂ and kidneys excrete HCO₃⁻/NH₄⁺ to keep blood at pH 7.4. Acidosis (pH down to ~7.1) / alkalosis (up to ~7.6): poor CO₂ exhalation → respiratory acidosis; hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis.

KCKey concepts

  • Water is polar and forms up to four hydrogen bonds; H-bonds are weak (~20 kJ/mol) but very numerous.
  • Noncovalent interactions: ionic interactions, hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces.
  • Polar and ionic substances dissolve in water by solvation (hydration).
  • The hydrophobic effect excludes nonpolar groups to maximize the entropy of water.
  • Amphiphiles form micelles or bilayers that bury hydrophobic groups.
  • Osmosis moves water; diffusion moves solutes down their concentration gradient.
  • Kw = 10⁻¹⁴; pH = −log[H⁺]; pH = pK + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
  • Buffers work best within ±1 pH unit of their pK; blood is buffered by bicarbonate.

QSelf-check

Self-check questions (8)

Answer in your head first, then tap the blank.

  1. Why is ice less dense than liquid water?

    → Each molecule makes 4 H-bonds in an open hexagonal lattice

  2. What drives the hydrophobic effect?

    → The increase in entropy of water when nonpolar groups aggregate

  3. Red blood cells are placed in pure water. What happens and why?

    → They swell and burst — water enters by osmosis (hypotonic)

  4. Calculate the pH of a solution with [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴ M.

    → 4

  5. An acetate buffer (pK 4.76) has [acetate] = 10 × [acetic acid]. pH?

    → 4.76 + log 10 = 5.76

  6. Which phosphate pK is useful for buffering near pH 7?

    → pK₂ = 6.82 (H₂PO₄⁻ ⇌ HPO₄²⁻)

  7. Hyperventilation causes which acid–base disturbance?

    → Respiratory alkalosis (CO₂ lost too quickly)

  8. In dialysis, what crosses the membrane?

    → Water and small solutes (not macromolecules)
